en: Majjhima Nikāya 19:
The Discourse on Two Kinds of Thought (Dvedhāvitakkasutta) Thus have I heard:
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, before my awakening, while I was still an unawakened bodhisatta, this thought occurred to me:”
‘What if I were to dwell having divided my thoughts into two groups? Then,
monks, I made those that were sensual thoughts, those that were thoughts of ill will, and those that were thoughts of cruelty into one group.
And whatever thought of renunciation, whatever thought of non-ill will, and whatever thought of non-cruelty—
this I made into my second portion. Yet, monks,
while I was dwelling thus diligent, ardent, and resolute, a thought of sensual desire arose in me.
Thus I understand:
"This sensual thought has arisen in me.
It leads to my own affliction, it leads to the affliction of others, and it leads to the affliction of both; it obstructs wisdom, belongs to the side of vexation, and does not conduce to Nibbāna."
“Monks, as I reflected, ‘This leads to harm for oneself,’ it subsided within me;
as I reflected, ‘This leads to harm for others,’ it subsided within me;
as I reflected, ‘This leads to harm for both,’ it subsided within me.”
“Monks, as I reflected: ‘It leads to the cessation of wisdom, it belongs to the side of affliction, and it does not conduce to Nibbāna,’ that [thought] vanished from me.
Monks, whatever sensual thought arose, I abandoned it, dispelled it, and brought it to an end.
While I was dwelling thus—heedful, ardent, and resolute—monks, a thought of ill will arose in me... [and so on].”
A thought of cruelty arises.
He understands thus:
"This thought of cruelty has arisen in me."

"And yet, it leads to one's own affliction, it leads to the affliction of others, and it leads to the affliction of both; it obstructs wisdom, belongs to the side of vexation, and does not conduce to Nibbāna.
Monks, as I reflected, "It leads to one's own affliction," this [thought] subsided within me;
as I reflected, "It leads to the affliction of others," this too subsided within me.
“Monks, when I reflected, ‘This leads to harm for both,’ it subsided within me;
and when I reflected, ‘It obstructs wisdom, belongs to the side of affliction, and does not lead to Nibbāna,’ it subsided within me.
Thus, monks, whenever a thought of cruelty arose, I abandoned it, I removed it, and I brought it to an end.”
“Bhikkhus, whatever a bhikkhu frequently thinks about and ponders upon, his mind inclines toward that very thing.

If a bhikkhu frequently thinks about and ponders upon thoughts of sensual desire, he has abandoned thoughts of renunciation and cultivated thoughts of sensual desire; thus his mind inclines toward those thoughts of sensual desire.
If, bhikkhus, he frequently thinks about and ponders upon thoughts of ill will …” [and so on].

“Bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu frequently thinks and ponders thoughts of cruelty, he has abandoned thoughts of non-cruelty and cultivated thoughts of cruelty; his mind inclines toward those thoughts of cruelty.

Just as, bhikkhus, in the last month of the rainy season, at the time of autumn, when the crops are thick in the field, a cowherd might guard his cattle by striking them here and there with a stick, prodding them, confining them, and driving them back.”
For what reason?
Because, monks, that cowherd sees that on account of it there might be death, imprisonment, loss, or blame.
In the same way, monks, I saw the danger, the degradation, and the defilement of unwholesome states; and I saw the benefit of renunciation and the side of purification in wholesome states.
“Monks, as I was dwelling thus—heedful, ardent, and resolute—an aspiration for renunciation arose in me.
I understood thus:
‘This aspiration for renunciation has indeed arisen in me.’”

"And yet, this does not lead to one's own affliction, nor does it lead to the affliction of others, nor does it lead to the affliction of both; rather, it increases wisdom, belongs to the side of non-affliction, and leads to Nibbāna.
Monks, even if I were to reflect upon and contemplate this throughout the night, I see no danger arising from that cause.
Monks, even if I were to reflect upon and contemplate this throughout the day, I see no danger arising from that cause."
“Monks, even if I were to reflect upon and examine this day and night, I do not see any danger arising from that cause.
However, if I were to reflect and examine it for too long, my body would become weary;
when the body is weary, the mind becomes agitated.”
"When the mind wanders, the mind is far from concentration.
Therefore, monks, I steady my own mind within, settle it, unify it, and concentrate it.
For what reason?
‘May my mind not be disturbed.
While I was dwelling thus, monks—heedful, ardent, and resolute—there arose in me a thought of non-ill will...
[and so on] ...there arose in me a thought of non-cruelty.
Thus I understand:
"This thought of non-harming has arisen in me.
And it leads neither to my own affliction, nor to the affliction of others, nor to the affliction of both; it increases wisdom, belongs to the side of non-affliction, and conduces to Nibbāna."
“Monks, even if I were to reflect upon and examine this throughout the night, I see no danger arising from that cause.
Monks, even if I were to reflect upon and examine this throughout the day, I see no danger arising from that cause.
Monks, even if I were to reflect upon and examine this throughout both night and day, I see no danger arising from that cause.”
Moreover, if I were to keep on thinking and pondering for too long, my body would grow weary;
when the body is weary, the mind becomes agitated;
and when the mind is agitated, it is far from concentration.
Thus, monks, I steadied my mind within myself, settled it, unified it, and concentrated it.
For what reason?
“Lest my mind be carried away.”
“Monks, whatever a monk frequently reflects upon and ponders, his mind inclines in that very direction.

If, monks, a monk frequently reflects upon and ponders thoughts of renunciation, he has abandoned thoughts of sensual desire; he has cultivated thoughts of renunciation extensively, and thus his mind inclines toward those thoughts of renunciation.
If, monks, he frequently reflects upon and ponders thoughts of non-ill will... [and so on].”

“Bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu frequently thinks and ponders upon thoughts of non-violence, he has abandoned thoughts of violence; he has cultivated thoughts of non-violence frequently, and his mind inclines toward those thoughts of non-violence.

Just as, bhikkhus, in the last month of summer, when all the crops have been gathered into the village, a cowherd guarding cattle would have nothing else to attend to while sitting at the foot of a tree or in the open air but this:
‘These are the cattle.’”
"In the same way, monks, there was only this to be done by mindfulness:
'These are the phenomena.
And, monks, my energy was aroused and unflagging; my mindfulness was established and unconfused; my body was tranquil and unagitated; and my mind was concentrated and one-pointed."

Thus, monks, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, I entered and dwelt in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion.

With the subsiding of thought and examination, I entered and dwelt in the second jhāna, which has internal tranquility and singleness of mind, is without thought and examination, and possesses rapture and happiness born of concentration.
And with the fading away of rapture, I dwelt equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending; I experienced happiness with the body.
I entered and dwelt in the third jhāna, which the Noble Ones describe as: “Equanimous, mindful, and dwelling in happiness.

With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, I entered and dwelt in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.

When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed it toward the knowledge of recollecting past lives.
I recollected my manifold past lives, that is: one birth... [as before] ...thus with their aspects and particulars, I recollected my manifold past lives.
This, monks, was the first true knowledge attained by me in the first watch of the night.
Ignorance was dispelled and true knowledge arose; darkness was dispelled and light arose, as happens for one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute.

When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed it toward the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings.
With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, I saw beings passing away and being reborn.
...pe... "Indeed, these worthy beings were possessed of misconduct of body... pe...

Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, I see beings passing away and being reborn—lowly and exalted, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate; I recognize beings according to their karma."
“Monks, this was the second true knowledge attained by me in the middle watch of the night:
ignorance was dispelled and true knowledge arose; darkness was dispelled and light arose, as happens for one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute.

With my mind thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed it toward the knowledge of the destruction of the taints.”
Thus I directly knew, as it really is: "This is suffering"; I directly knew, as it really is:

"This is the origin of suffering"; I directly knew, as it really is: "This is the cessation of suffering"; I directly knew, as it really is: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering."
‘These are the taints,’ I understood as it really is; ‘this is the origin of the taints,’ I understood as it really is;
‘this is the cessation of the taints,’ I understood as it really is; ‘this is the way leading to the cessation of the taints,’ I understood as it really is.

As I knew thus and saw thus, my mind was liberated from the influx of sensual desire, my mind was liberated from the influx of existence, and my mind was liberated from the influx of ignorance. When it was liberated, there came the knowledge: "It is liberated.
I directly realized: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
This, monks, was the third true knowledge attained by me in the last watch of the night.
Ignorance has been dispelled and true knowledge has arisen; darkness has been dispelled and light has arisen, as happens for one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute.
Just as, monks, there might be a great low-lying marsh in a forest glade, and a great herd of deer were living in dependence upon it.
Then some man might appear who desires their harm, their disadvantage, and their lack of security from bondage.
He would block the path that is safe, auspicious, and delightful; he would open up a wrong path, set out a trap, and place a snare.
In this way, monks, that great herd of deer would eventually meet with ruin and disaster.
But suppose, monks, a certain man were to arise who desired their welfare, desired their benefit, and desired their security from bondage.
He would reveal to them that path which is secure, leading to well-being, and delightful; he would close off the wrong path, drive away the deer-trapper, and destroy the deer-trapper’s snare.
In this way, monks, that great herd of deer would, after some time, attain growth, increase, and abundance.
This simile, monks, has been employed by me for the purpose of making the meaning clear.
And this is the meaning here:
"A great low-lying marsh," monks, is a designation for sensual pleasures.
“‘A great herd of deer,’ monks, is a designation for sentient beings.
‘A man who desires what is unbeneficial, who desires what is harmful, who desires what is not the security from bondage,’ monks, is a designation for Māra the Evil One.
‘A wrong path,’ monks, is a designation for the eightfold wrong path, namely:”
Of wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration.
"Roaming about" (okacara), monks, is a designation for delight-and-lust (nandīrāga).
"A roamer" (okacārikā), monks, is a designation for ignorance (avijjā).
“‘A person who desires welfare, who desires benefit, who desires security from bondage’—this, monks, is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
‘The secure path, leading to well-being, bringing joy’—this, monks, is a designation for the Noble Eightfold Path; that is to say:
right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.”
“Thus, monks, the secure path leading to well-being and bringing joy has been opened by me; the wrong path has been closed off, the haunt cleared away, and the prowler driven out.
Whatever was to be done for disciples by a teacher seeking their welfare, out of compassion and motivated by kindness—that has been done by me for you.
Here, monks, are the roots of trees; here are empty huts. Meditate, monks, do not be negligent, lest you later fall into regret. This is my instruction to you.”
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
The bhikkhus were satisfied and rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The ninth discourse, "The Two Kinds of Thought," is concluded.
